The country edition of the Examiner of yesterday contained the important correspondence between Generals Grant and Lee, near Richmond, which ended in the surrender of the whole army of the latter to the former. With the exception of a small force under General Johnston in North Carolina the rebel government has now no organized military force of any importance in the field east of Mississippi River. This SURRENDER, therefore, is in all probability, the final of the great military events of the war which bids fair to end in the complete subjugation of the secession States to the power of the Federal arms. After the consequences which followed the surrender of General Joe Johnston—the idiotic march of Hood into Tennessee and the defeat and destruction of his army by Thomas; the unopposed progress of Sherman through Georgia and the Carolinas; the fall of Savannah, Charleston, Wilmington and Richmond this result will not be unexpected by our readers.

In view of the hopelessness of the struggle, it was the act of wisdom on the part of Gen. Lee not to needlessly prolong it, and cause further destruction of life and devastation of property in his section, already so terribly impoverished and ruined.

Whether this surrender is made with the consent of the Richmond Government, or, whether fleeing beyond the Mississippi River into the remote and almost inaccessible State of Texas, the latter will continue for some time yet to prolong the struggle there is a question yet to be determined. But this side of the Mississippi the war is apparently over, and we are now brought face to face with the work of political Reorganization. When the soldier has finished his task, the work of the statesman begins. The aim, of course, will be to heal the calamities of the war, to repair the ruin it has wrought, and cause the Southern people once more to fulfill their functions with cheerfulness in the Union. This, it will be conceded by all, is a work of immense difficulty, and requires for its successful performance the highest ability and greatest wisdom.

We copy, this morning, a very interesting letter from the Secretary of the Treasury to Henry G. Carey, Esq, the distinguished Pennsylvania Economist. We infer from the tenor of Secretary McCulloch's letter that he was in receipt of letter from Mr. Carey, complaining of the sudden decline in gold, and urging the Treasury Department not to precipitate return to specie payment lest it should ruin the manufacturing interests of the country.

The continued whining of the Pennsylvania Manufacturers for protection and encouragement is getting to sound very disagreeably in Northwestern ears. From the foundation of the Government, large portion of the time and attention of the different Congresses have been occupied by the manufacturing interests of Pennsylvania and the New England States. They are, always, if we place implicit confidence in the statements of their mouthpieces, upon the verge of bankruptcy and destruction, and unless the people of the country are taxed for their benefit, the nation is forever ruined. It is quite notorious that the Manufacturers of Pennsylvania and New England have during the past three years, realized fortunes, before which the exploits of Aladdin's wonderful lamp pale into insignificance. By the unparalleled advance in all of their articles—the taxes levied by the Government in a great many instances going into their pockets in addition—their wealth has become fabulous. Now, when there is a prospect of decline in goods, and indications are seen that they will have to lose some of their hastily and easily acquired wealth by that decline, they are besieging the Treasury Department, and will no doubt be blockading the doors of the next Congress, for relief from impending destruction. We trust the representatives from the Northwest will no longer be imposed upon by this clamor. There is no reason that we discover why manufacturers alone should be entitled to all the advantages of an extraordinary advance in all their wares, and be protected from the disadvantages of corresponding decline.

Secretary McCulloch discusses the question of a reduction of the currency in plain language and with decided ability. While he insists that resumption of specie payments is with him a cardinal point, he does not propose to bring about the event by such a curtailment of the currency as would prostrate or injuriously affect those great interests upon the prosperity of which the Government depends for its revenue, and which cannot be broken down or severely depressed without depriving labor of its proper reward. The Secretary is aware that, among those whose habits of personal indulgence lead them into protracted excesses, sobering is a dangerous experiment; but dangerous as it may be, he regards it as preferable to continued intoxication.

The views of Secretary McCulloch are worthy the thoughtful consideration of all classes. It is very apparent, from his language, that he designs to bring back the country to a specie basis at the earliest practicable moment consistent with the best interest of all classes of the community.

We are thankful to President Lincoln for giving us a Secretary of the Treasury whose ideas are not bigot-bound by an education obtained among the men of the past.

It is surprising how tenaciously unjust Power and Privilege have clung to the smallest shadow of what they call their rights: and now ready they have always been to resist interference even to the point of destruction to the weaker party.

The heavy armed legions of Rome came in contact with every variety of nations on the three continents; and at the time of Augustus, out of a population of 100,000,000, one half were slaves. The modern historian sympathizes with the deplorable condition of large part of these wretched beings, on whom the naughty master and mistress were educated to look down with the same cold indifference with which they regarded their cattle on the farms. Great numbers could be seen at work, chained together in companies; and as the Romans their labors were often of the severest kind in preparing the new lands.

EDITOR CHRONICLE: The bounty substitute broker bill was signed on Monday and became the law. It caused quite scatterment amongst the fraternity. These fellows had usurped nearly the entire business, making large profits out of the community subject to draft buying up men at low figures and selling them out at high ones—pocketing the difference. Not only that, but getting the worst class of men for substitutes, bounty jumpers suiting them as well as any. All they cared for was the profit. It has been said that they were willing to give over one hundred thousand dollars to defeat the bill. If the Bill has the effect intended—it is worth more to the people and the country, than to have saved the expense of this winter's Legislation.

Mr. Davis, the Clerk of the Senate, who was captured in the South and for some time in Salisbury prison, North Carolina, entertained the Senate and House on Tuesday evening in the Hall of the House with narrative of his experience. It was enough to make the blood run cold to hear of the barbarities practised upon our soldiers. Starving them, not because they had not the food for them, but to compel them to enlist in the Southern army, and some of them were so famished as to go and some poor fellows accepting the terms, so far exhausted as to die before being mustered in. He was followed by Governor Brough, who stated that he was present at the landing of some of our exchanged prisoners at Baltimore, and witnessed the death of nine of our men, who died in the transfer from the boat to the Hospital, very short distance. Thus have our men been treated by these worse than barbarians—claiming more Christianity and a higher civilization than we possess. Henceforth let the terms "Southern Chivalry," and "Southern Hospitality" be stencil and offense to every man, having only the common instincts of humanity. There is no man of the North who is not the superior of the chiefest of them. But the veiled prophet is being uncovered and his hideousness and deformity appears to him who behold. No tongue has told, no pen described, the horror, the iniquity, the degradation connected with the accursed institution of slavery. But brighter day dawning—is here. Congress has deliberated, and acted to purpose, the shackles fall, not only from those now living, but for all future generations. PLAIEs.-A dispatch received at Gen.
Dodges headquarters, ST. Louis, states
that the emigration across the plains
this season far exceeds that of any pre-
vious year. During the month of May
four thousand wagons passed Fort Kear-
ney, and trains continued to pass that
post in large numbers The emigrants
are bound for Idaho, Montana, Salt
Lake, California, and other places. The
Indians had not molestsd the emigrants
to any noticeable extent, and all the
routes are considered safe. Troops are
stationed at the various posts, and afford
ample protection to the trains.

Mrs. Lincoln, Miss Harris, and Major Rathburn,
was shot by an assassin who suddenly entered the
box. He approached behind the President. The
assassin then leaped upon the stage, brandishing
a large dagger or knife, and made his escape by the
rear of the theatre. The pistol ball entered the
back of the President's head. The wound is mortal; the President has been insensible very since
it was inflicted, and is now dying.

About the same hour an assassin, either the same
or another, entered Mr. Seward's house, and, under
pretense of having a prescription, was shown
to the Secretary's sick chamber. The Secretary
was in bed, nurse and Miss Seward with him.
The assassin immediately rushed to the bed, inflicted
two or three stabs to the throat, and two on the
face. It is hoped the wounds may not be mortal,
but apprehension is that they will prove fatal. The
nurse alarmed Mr. Frederick Seward, who was in
an adjoining room, and fastened to the door of his
father's room, where he met the assassin, who in
inflicted upon him one or more dangerous wounds.
The recovery of Frederick Seward is doubtful.

It is not probable that the President will live
through the night.

General Grant and wife were advertised to be at
the theatre this evening, but the latter started to
Burlington at six o'clock last evening.

At Cabinet meeting at which General Grant
was present to-day, the subject of the state of the
country, and the prospects of speedy peace was
discussed. The President was very cheerful and
honestly spoke very kindly of General Lee and
others of the Confederacy, and the establishment
of Government in Virginia. All the members of the
Cabinet, except Mr. Seward, are now in attendance upon the President. I have seen Mr.
Seward, but he and Frederick were both unconscious. EDWIN M. STANTON,

Secretary of War.

"I rather think I do," said Pelatiah; "she's my wife."

"For wife!" cried the other. "She is mine before God and man, Anna Matson, and she is the mother of my children."

"And mine too," said Pelatiah. "I left her with baby in her arms. If you are David Matson, your right to her is outlawed; at any rate she is mine, and I am not the man to give her up."

SIXTH VOLUME.
THE Fire Lands Historical Society proposes to publish
the Sixth Volume on or before the Second Wednesday
of June next. It will be of the enlarged size containing
not less than one hundred twenty-four pages and issued
in neat quarto for double columns, clear type, fine paper
and in the same attractive style as the previous volumes.


Price 50 Cents, payable in advance.
It will contain selections from the valuable historical
matter gathered by the Society, among which are the
official proceedings of its meetings held during the year at
Norwalk, Perkins, and Monroeville; Historical collections
of Perkins and Danbury (ready); The capture,
trial, and execution of the Indians Negosheek and Ne-
gonaba for the murder of Bishop and Wood on the Pen-
insula in 1815; The Journal of John Garrison, the first
white settler of Sandusky; The Survey of the Fire Lands
in 1826, written by Simeon Hoyt of the party; The
biography of each member of the Society, with residence
and place of BIRTH, when and where first settled on the Fire
Lands, and finely engraved Portrait of the late Hon.
Eleutheros Cooke.
Subscriptions may be made at the Journal Office, Fran-
cton, or to F. D. Parish, Sandusky, Philip Rossi,
T. N. Schuyler, G. A. Preston, H. H. Pease.

Johnson, Grant and Sherman on Negro

The Milwaukee Journal feels authorized
to say, that the democracy of Wisconsin
are deeply indebted to Senator Doolittle
for his argument in this city on Monday
evening, in opposition to the views of the
republican party and his candidates for
state officers. We feel especially indebted
to the Senator for the assurance that
the opinions of Generals Grant and Sher-
man, as well as these of President Johnson,
fully accord with those entertained
and declared by the democracy of Wisconsin
in their state platform. Below we
give his statements as to the recently ex-
pressed opinions of the distinguished gen-
tlemen we have named:


PRESIDENT JOHNSON on NEGRO SUFFRAGE.


Referring to a recent interview between
himself and President Johnson, Senator
Doolittle said:


Mr. Johnson was decidedly of the
opinion that if he as President of the Uni-
ted States, in the present condition of the
prejudices—almost haired, if you please—
existing between the two races—if he
were to insist that suffrage should be
granted to the negro population there as
a condition precedent to their being re-
cognized as states in the Union, it would
produce actual war between the blacks
and the whites. Mr. Johnson has lived
there all his life. He has been governor
of Tennessee and he knows what he talks
about.


GEN. GRANT on NEGRO SUFFRAGE.


Senator Doolittle continued:


But will not stop here. This is too
serious for men with flippant tongues to
pass over as if there was nothing in it.
The other day when Gen. Grant was here,
while spending several hours with him in
free conversation upon this subject, he ex-
pressed to me his opinion. Said I, Gen.
Grant, never quote private conversation
without permission. Am I permitted to
state what you now state? He said,
certainly, there is no concealment on
my part and he stated to me in that con-
versation that a considerable portion
of the troubles between the whites and
the blacks was on account of this unwiso
attempt to force negro suffrage in these
states. He said further, that if the federal
government were to attempt to do it, it
would undoubtedly produce war between
the two races there.


GEN. SHERMAN ON NEGRO SUFFRAGE.


As to Gen. Sherman's opinions on this
question, Senator Doolittle said:


How does it seem for some of your
young men—young men who have never
been there in their lives, and who know
nothing about it, some editor of a news-
paper, for instance, in view of authority
like this, to say that it means nothing
when I stand up before the people and
seek to save the lives of these poor down-
trodden colored men whom their mistaken
zeal and false philanthropy, their blinded
fanaticism would hurry into their graves
by hundreds and thousands perhaps?
(Applause) And there is another thing,
fellow citizens—that great captain who
was this day in the city, and who desired
much to be present here this evening
whose friends telegraphed to Chicago &c.
detain the boat that he might come here
but were unable to do so—that great
captain, who at the head of his conqueror
legions, swept through the very heart of
the rebellion—has lived in Louisiana
and was teaching school there at the
time the rebellion broke out—he, too, in
conversation with me at Madison, deliver-
ed precisely the opinion of Gen. Grant,
and gave me the same permission to speak
of it.


SENATOR DOOLITTLE ON NEGRO SUFFRAGE


The Senator's own opinion on the sub-
ject is presented in the following
paragraphs:


Now fellow citizens, when I stand here
pleading against this insane object—for it
is none other—of insisting that the gov-
ernment of the United States shall force
negro suffrage upon the people at the
south at this time and render these cir-
cumstances, I state to you not my opinion
but the opinion of those men who have
been there and who know the effects.
And he must be a very brave man who
has never been there and knows nothing
about it, but stands up and says there is
no foundation for it. (Applause) Why,
fellow citizens, we read about the war in
Haiti—what is that war but a war of
races?

way of reminding the electors of the state

races at the south, by voting for the
democratic candidates at the coming elec-
tion. The democratic platform is the
only platform which accords with the
views of President Johnson, Gen. Grant,

Saffer, of the 9th Connecticut Volunteers

steamer from Liverpool. The prisoner was
found to have in his possession a seven bar-
reled revolver, 20 rounds of patent rifle
ball cartridges, also box of percussion caps,
four military drill books, four commissions,
bearing his name to serve in the Connecti-
cut Volunteers as Lieutenant and Colonel;

Bourse, 5 1/2%, flat. Rentes closed at 65

ation pay the expenses of the late Danish

pool having taken place on the 31st ult.,

respondent of the Times says that it is gen-
erally reported in partisan papers that the
French army in Mexico will be withdrawn
by installments, and that by August or Sep-
tember of next year the whole will have re-
turned to France. This resolution is said to

thence to Selma, thence down the Alabama
river to Cahaba. After a detention of four
days at this point, a detachment of Eve hundred
prisoners, including the officers and
men of the Seventeenth, were put on board
the Q. R. transport 'Coquette,' and started
up the river, bound for eastern prisons. On
the tenth of October they arrived at Mont-
gomer, and were transferred to railroad
train, bound for Columbus, Ga., which lat-
ter point they reached the next afternoon at
2 o'clock. During the ride from Montgom-
ery to Columbus, Capt. Deal and Capt. J. T.
Skelton of the same regiment, made up their
minds to escape if possible, and agreed upon a
plan of operations. The last named officer
had been in captivity about a year before,
and had effected his escape from Libby Pri-
son after series of bold adventures and
hairbreadth escapes. When the train ar-
rived at Columbus, the prisoners were park-
ed in a common near the Macon railroad de-
pot. Captains Deal and Shelton proposed
to the guard to have a fire kindled, and
while pretending to be gathering fuel for
that purpose, they lodged from the pres-
ence of the sentinel, and disappeared into the
darkness. Knowing they would be follow-
ed as soon as missed, and that the presump-
tion would be that they would set out in the
direction of Atlanta, they proceeded north-
ward, till they struck the Chattahoochee ri-
ver, thence proceeded down the river, and
finally a complete circuit of the city, travel-
ing as much as possible in water so as to
throw the bloodhounds from the track, in
case that style of pursuers should be put
upon their heels. Having thus baffled what-
ever measures might have been taken in
camp to recapture them, they proceeded
cautiously down the river, crawling on their
hands and knees in some instances through
the thick and almost impenetrable cane-
breaks by day, and taking to the open fields
when they thought it prudent, by night.
In this manner they travelled forty miles,
until they reached the plantation of Gabriel
Toombs, relative (we think brother) of Rob-
ert Toombs. Here they obtained from a
body servant of the Ex-G. Georgia U. S. Sena-
tor, a bateau, for their transportation down
the river. The servant was suffering se-
verely from illness, but at great personal
risk he conducted the fugitives some three
miles along the river bank to where the boat
lay, although in accomplishing the journey
he was compelled frequently to sit down and
rest. He obtained for them about three
days supply of bread, and asked nothing
for the boat, bread, or his own services; but
the officers insisted upon his acceptance of
a silver watch, to which he finally consent-
ed. Bidding their friend adieu, they em-
barked in bateau, but had proceeded only a
short distance, when they ran into DIN,
and Captain Skelton was precipitated into the
stream, and had a narrow escape from
drowning. He finally grasped the edge of
the boat, and with the assistance of his com-
panion was enabled to get on shore. Re-
pairing damages as far as possible, they
started again, but had proceeded only a
short distance, before their frail boat sprang
a leak, and threatened them with new
danger. Captain Skelton had only two pairs
of pantaloons, and parting with one of them,
material was thus obtained for caulking the
bateau. And after effecting the repairs, the
voyagers again proceeded downstream.
They found the country on either side of the
river for two hundred and eighty miles one
continuous cornfield, and of course passed
at short distances planters' houses and neg-
ro huts. Through this region they could
only proceed at night hauling their boat in
the cane-breaks and concealing themselves
